20074-the-story-of-the-cambrian-a-biogra:
C. P. Gasquoine wrote The Story of the Cambrian, a biography of a railway in Wales. Railways rarely get life stories, yet the Cambrian lines had a long, hard one. Gasquoine thanks many friends tied to the Cambrian Railways for their help. Their aid made even an attempt at the tale possible, he says.

Inside are lines, stations, firms, and the men who ran them. Welsh hills and coastal towns shaped every mile of track. The book records growth, strain, and change in one rail system. Readers who love rail history get names, dates, and local detail in depth.
20164-critical-miscellanies-vol-1-of-3-e:
John Morley wrote Critical Miscellanies, and volume one holds an essay on Macaulay. Morley was a leading critic and statesman of Victorian Britain. He praises the habit of writing down what one reads and thinks. Such notes give learning clearness, shape, and a right place, he says.

Macaulay, the famed historian and essayist, is a fit subject for Morley. Both men wrote prose of great force and wide public reach. The essay weighs Macaulay's gifts, faults, and place in English letters. Readers get two sharp Victorian minds meeting on the page at once.
20201-mary-gray:
Mary Gray is a novel of a girl raised in a poor London street. Her home was one of a squat line of mean little houses. Those houses hid behind a great church in the city's heart. The road before them led only to the church's back entrance.

From such narrow ground, Mary Gray's life and choices unfold. Poverty, work, and love test girls in tales of this kind. The church at her back stands as both shelter and shadow. Readers get a sober city novel on a poor girl's path to womanhood.
20575-my-dog-tray:
My Dog Tray is a story in verse and prose for children, about a poor girl named Nelly and her faithful dog. Tray never leaves her side. At night, while Nelly's tears are shed in hushed sorrow, the dog crouches close to keep her warm.

With pitying love, Tray licks her bitter tears away. Nelly shares her crusts with him, and he shares her hard life with a dog's steady heart. Tales like this one, of animal faithfulness to a suffering child, were nursery favorites in the Victorian years. Tray's devotion carries the whole lesson of the book.
20736-the-girl-scouts-at-home-or-rosanna:
Katherine Keene Galt wrote Rosanna's Beautiful Day for the Girl Scouts at Home set of tales. One scene shows a big garage, fit for four cars, wrapped in vines. Its one door opens into a garden, with no other door or window on that side.

Rosanna's day turns small home events into a full, happy arc for young readers. Scouting values of help, cheer, and care run through the tale. The book shows how early Scout fiction brought the movement into ordinary homes. It keeps a light touch, with family scenes and outdoor touches in equal share.
21116-the-easiest-way:
Eugene Walter's play The Easiest Way became this 1911 novel, written with Arthur Hornblow as a story of metropolitan life. Its heroine, Laura Murdock, calls herself an actress, though the foreword insists she has no talent for the stage. She has lived as a kept woman and wants to change.

Laura tries to redeem her past through an honest, unselfish love. The attempt fails badly, and she falls back toward the easy way of the title. The authors stress that working actors should not be judged by Laura's type. Broadway crowds and New York rooms frame her rise and collapse.
21228-white-lilac-or-the-queen-of-the-ma:
Amy Walton's story for girls begins with Mrs White at her cottage door. She is anxious about a promised visit from the rector's wife to see the new baby. Several of her children have died, so this one matters all the more. A branch of white lilac, brought by her husband, gives the baby her name: Lilac White.

Her father dies soon after, and her mother raises her alone. At twelve Lilac is pretty enough for a visiting artist to want her in a picture, until a cousin's new hair-do spoils the sitting. May Day brings rivalry over Queen of the May, and grief follows close behind the honour.
21267-lincoln-s-birthday:
Robert Haven Schauffler edited this anthology for the Our American Holidays series, published in New York in 1909 and reprinted through 1916. It promises a full view of Lincoln through the most noteworthy essays, orations, and poems about him, plus fiction and Lincoln's own writings. Thanksgiving and Christmas volumes stand beside it in the series.

Schools and families used such anthologies to mark February 12 with readings rather than only ceremony. Pieces from many ages and nations show Lincoln as others saw him: speaker, president, and folk hero. The editor thanks many publishers for permissions. It is a period piece of Lincoln devotion, gathered for one day a year.
21758-hudson-bay:
In May 1841, a letter changed young R. M. Ballantyne's life: he was appointed apprentice clerk to the Hudson's Bay Company. This book is his own account of the years that followed, in the fur country of Canada. In his preface he says his chief aim is the everyday life of that world, a subject other writers had only touched in passing.

The pages follow the daily work of the trade: the outposts, the Red River Settlement, the travel, and the long winters. Later editions kept the text nearly as written, since the far posts changed so slowly. Every novel Ballantyne later wrote about the north grew from these years. As memoir, it is the seed of them all.
21782-the-yillian-way:
Jame Retief, vice-consul in Earth's Diplomatic Corps, faces the most polite danger in the galaxy in Keith Laumer's The Yillian Way. The Yill of the title are gray-skinned hosts whose ceremonial protocol is impressive, colorful, and, in the long run, deadly. Retief watches a Yill party where a raised fist and hands on a head pass for friendly custom. Every gesture means something, and a wrong one could kill.

The ambassador's staff insists that Terrestrials are a kindly, peace-loving race. Retief, junior and sharp-eyed, must work the mission in harmony while the Yill smile and sip lavender drinks. Laumer builds the tale on manners as warfare. It is a sly, funny story of diplomacy where etiquette itself is the trap.
21836-the-tale-of-jasper-jay:
Jasper Jay, the noisiest rogue in Pleasant Valley, stars in this 1917 children's tale by Arthur Scott Bailey. Some birds called old Mr. Crow the loudest in the neighborhood, but they had forgotten his knavish cousin. Jasper's shrieks ring over Farmer Green's pines on the coldest mornings, for he winters right there. He is bold and handsome in his bright blue suit, and a rogue for all that.

Chapters follow his jokes, boasts, and narrow escapes: scaring the hens, hiding from Solomon Owl, and joining the singing society. Bailey's Tuck-Me-In Tales teach nature through animal mischief. Jasper has to be got rid of more than once, and never quite is. Small readers learn the blue jay by laughing at him.
21846-crowded-out-o-crofield-or-the-boy-:
Jack Ogden, a blacksmith's boy in the village of Crofield, is crowded out into the wide world in this boys' novel by William O. Stoddard. Stoddard insists the tale is close to history: a real energetic boy was pushed from his village into a surprising career. Jack stands fifteen, sandy-haired and freckled, in the wide door of the smithy, looking toward the rickety bridge.

His road runs down the Hudson by steamboat, past the state-house, into the city and a new world. Chapters bring a runaway, a burglary charge, hunger, and work at all trades before complete success. Mary, the girl of the tale, sails her own course in the Eagle. It is a cheerful American success story of the old school.
22141-joy-in-service-forgetting-and-pres:
Joy in Service, issued by the American Tract Society in 1900, is a devotional book about the Christian life. Its full title runs Forgetting and Pressing Onward Until the Day Dawn. The writer argues that knowing Christ in history is not enough. A believer may admire Christ's power and adore him as Saviour, yet still long for a closer, personal acquaintance with him.

The chapters press readers toward active service done with joy. Forgetting what lies behind, they are to strain forward like Paul. Tract Society books were cheap, earnest, and everywhere in Protestant America. This one survives as a fair sample of the devotional reading that shaped ordinary churchgoers in 1900.
22267-a-woman-for-mayor-a-novel-of-to-da:
Helen M. Winslow, once editor of The Club Woman, wrote A Woman for Mayor as a novel of to-day in 1909. Her city, the talk runs, is going to the dogs. Municipal affairs were never so muddled, everybody agrees. Barnaby Burke is running for mayor with a ravenous pack of demagogues behind him, and honest citizens despair of the result.

Against Burke the reformers set a woman candidate. Winslow, who knew clubwomen and suffrage circles from inside, builds her plot on ward politics, newspapers, and drawing-room pressure. The question is whether a woman can clean a city hall. The novel is a suffrage argument wearing a story's clothes, lively and pointed.
22271-schwartz-a-history-from-schwartz-b:
Schwartz: A History is the title novel of David Christie Murray's linked volume Schwartz. Its narrator opens with a startling sentence: he was expatriated by a man with an axe. The man and the axe alike were visionary and unreal, he admits. Yet it took a strong effort of will to hold them at arm's length. Work on hand, and a mind broken down by overwork, explain the vision.

Murray builds the history out of that haunted start. Business, exile, and a disordered conscience drive Schwartz's story. The linked tales that follow share his world of Castle Barfield and London counting-houses. This opening piece shows Murray blending the ghostly with the commercial.
22273-bulldog-and-butterfly-from-schwart:
Bulldog and Butterfly, from David Christie Murray's Schwartz, opens with a map in words. Castle Barfield, Heydon Hey, and Beacon Hargate form three points of a triangle. Barfield has pretensions; Heydon Hey is a village; Beacon Hargate is no more than a hamlet. The house at the story's centre is crossed by great beams of black-painted oak, with diamond-paned windows sunk low in the walls.

Roses and honeysuckle cover the porch in summer, and the garden runs up to the house all round. Murray sets his contrast of bulldog and butterfly in this old place. Character against character, as the title promises, drives the slight tale. The Schwartz stories share this countryside.
22417-the-etiquette-of-to-day:
The Etiquette of To-Day, revised and enlarged in 1918, teaches the manners of its moment. It opens by naming the secret of success in society. That secret, it says, is heartiness and sympathy in company.

A man unhappy in company finds no fitting word ready. All his information sounds a little impertinent to others. A happy man finds lucky occasions at every turn. He introduces what he has to say with ease. The book builds its rules on that warm foundation. Calls, letters, dress, and table conduct follow in order. Readers get Edwardian-era social rules, useful now as a mirror of their world.
22720-the-minister-of-evil-the-secret-hi:
The Minister of Evil, subtitled The Secret History of Rasputin's Betrayal of Russia, is a 1917 insider's account of the fall of the Russian monarchy. The catalog record names no author. Its writer claims no literary renown and no pretence to fine phrases or elegant diplomacy.

The object, the author states plainly, is simply to set down the truth about Russia's crumbling and the fall of its throne. Rasputin, the Siberian holy man whose influence over the tsarina scandalized Russia, stands at the center as the minister of evil. Such books poured out in revolution's first year, mixing memoir, accusation, and grief. This one preserves the voice of a loyalist watching an empire dissolve.
22758-the-new-england-magazine-volume-1-:
The New England Magazine presents its second number, volume 1, number 2, dated February 1886. The catalog record names no editor. A new regional magazine had to prove itself monthly, and this issue again mixes college history, essays, and literature for New England readers.

The sample article traces the founding impulse of Tufts College to a single sermon. Hosea Ballou the younger preached it before the General Convention of Universalists. The place was New York, in September 1847. From a sermon to a college is the kind of story the magazine loved: faith, education, and regional ambition in one thread. Poetry and fiction fill out the number. Together with its first issue, it shows the Bay State Monthly settling into the long career ahead of it.
22913-winning-his-way:
Charles Carleton Coffin's Winning His Way follows travelers into a beautiful valley. After weeks on dusty roads they reach a winding river, fair sunny hills, and groves of oak, maple, and linden. The air smells of honeysuckle and jasmine, and deer browse the tender grass on the slopes.

Coffin wrote history and adventure for boys, and this tale mixes settlement, striving, and scenery. A young hero makes his path in a new country, learning work and character along the way. The valley scene shows Coffin's method, rewarding effort with a rich land honestly described. His books taught generations of readers their American past. This one keeps the same earnest, outdoors spirit.
23024-grimm-tales-made-gay:
Guy Wetmore Carryl retells the Grimms in verse in Grimm Tales Made Gay. One tale turns on a will. Four-year-old Paul stands to take half the gold, while Beatrix, six, inherits the remainder. Uncle Ben responds with an act everyone calls splendid.

Carryl's trick is to keep the fairy-tale skeleton and swap the moral for a wink. His rhymes bounce, his endings swerve, and his morals arrive upside down on purpose. The book belonged to a brief vogue for comic retellings around 1900. Children can follow the stories, adults catch the jokes aimed over their heads. It remains a neat sample of light verse at its most professional.
23086-auction-of-to-day:
Milton C. Work calls the bids in Auction of To-Day, his 1913 guide to auction bridge. Work starts from a simple position, one spade opened and second hand passing. Case follows case from there. Dealer strength, raises to two and three spades, and minor-suit openings each get their treatment.

Work was America's bridge authority, and this book taught a generation how to bid the new auction game. Hands, conventions, and probabilities fill its pages in place of plot. Card historians prize such manuals, since they fix the exact moment when contract bridge was still unborn and auction ruled the clubs. Casual readers will find a vanished social world, conducted in spades.
23207-americans-all-stories-of-american-:
Americans All, from 1910, presents stories of American life of its own day. Its pages open by praising school days as days rich in experience. The first day at school, whether a little red schoolhouse or a big brick building holding a thousand pupils, is called the start of a new life.

As a model of school fiction, the book points to Emmy Lou, by George Madden Martin. That story follows a winsome girl from first grade through the end of high school. Readers get period stories and sketches that treat ordinary American childhood, school, and home life as worthy subjects.
a-laodicean-a-story-of-to-day: Thomas Hardy's 1881 Laodicean: a story of today. A lukewarm lover in modern Wessex. The master's contemporary novel. Interesting and fine, hardy's modern Wessex novel, a lukewarm lover, interesting and fine, Hardy's contemporary novel, modern Wessex.
a-millionaire-of-yesterday: An Edward Phillips Oppenheim novel about a self-made millionaire and the dark secrets of his past. Money, mystery, and Edwardian high life unfold in the author's smooth, practiced style. Popular fiction of the first order, with machine-like plotting that never misses a beat.
a-narrative-of-the-expedition-to-botany-: Watkin Tench sailed with the First Fleet and wrote this firsthand record. His account covers the voyage to Botany Bay and the early camp at Sydney. Readers meet the land, the sea, and its first people. A priceless window on Australia's founding.
a-terrible-temptation-a-story-of-to-day:
A Terrible Temptation, subtitled A Story of To-Day, is an 1871 novel by Charles Reade. Reade was a leading Victorian novelist, famous for turning close research into dramatic stories of modern life. The subtitle is his signal: unlike his historical romances, this tale is set in the England of his own day, among its present manners and pressures.

As the title promises, the story turns on a temptation and the damage it threatens to those who face it. Reade builds his fiction on strong situations and moral stakes, and this novel applies that method to contemporary society. It stands in his output as his pointed look at the temptations of modern life, written for the readers who were living it.
a-wasted-day: A Richard Harding Davis story about a day gone wrong and the lessons it teaches. Light, human, and told with the author's easy charm, it finds meaning in small misadventures. A pleasant minor work. Davis finds the universal in the particular, with a light and practiced hand.
barriers-burned-away: Edward Payson Roe's breakthrough novel unfolds against the Great Chicago Fire of 1871, which literally burns away the barriers between his characters. Through romance tested by disaster, Roe preaches faith, honesty, and the chance to begin again. The book made him famous and remains a vivid picture of nineteenth-century American city life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-all-saints-da: A 1913 entry on All Saints' Day — the feast of November first. Francis Mershman traces its history. The Pantheon became Mary's church that day. All heaven is honored at once. The Church's great roll call. Its vigil was once a fast.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-all-souls-day: This 1913 reference article on All Souls' Day — the November second of holy remembrance. Francis Mershman tells its tender story. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ancient-see-o: This 1913 reference article on the ancient see of Bergen — Norway's western bishopric. Arthur Taylor gives its story. Its bishops served the Hanse town. The Reformation swept the old faith. A vanished see of the fjords. Its Mariakirken keeps the old stones.

catholic-encyclopedia-1913-du-coudray: A 1913 entry on Du Coudray — a French officer of note. Thomas Meehan records his American service. The entry preserves his modest fame. His sword served the colonial cause. A soldier of the revolutionary war. His Yorktown service is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edmund-and-jo: A 1913 entry on Edmund and John Hay — the Jesuit brothers. John Hungerford Pollen honors their martyred deaths. They died for the persecuted faith. The entry preserves their blessed memory. The martyrs of the English mission. Their 1579 martyrdom is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-family-of-har: A 1913 entry on the Harlay — the French parlementaires. Georges Goyau notes their famous line. The entry preserves their modest record. Their robes graced the Paris courts. A house of the seventeenth century. Their 1616 presidency is famed.

catholic-encyclopedia-1913-galloway: This 1913 reference piece on Galloway — the Scottish diocese. William Turner gives its ancient story. Its bishops serve the southwestern flock. The Solway guards the old town. A see of the Scottish borders. Its 1878 diocese is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gaudete-sunda: This 1913 reference article on Gaudete Sunday — the rose Sunday. George Cyprian Alston unfolds its joyful rite. Rejoice crowns the Advent's midst. The vestments blush the rose hue. The respite of the penitential season. Its third Advent is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-day: This 1913 reference article on George Day — the Bishop of Chichester. George Phillips notes his famous see. The entry preserves his modest fame. His rule served the sixteenth century. A prelate of the Tudor age. His 1556 death is famed.

catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-pray: A 1913 entry on György Pray — the Hungarian historian. Antal Aldásy honors his famous annals. His pen chronicled the Magyar kings. The scholars mine the learned tomes. The Baronius of the Hungarian Church. His 1801 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-good-friday: A 1913 entry on Good Friday — the day of the Cross. Thomas Gilmartin unfolds its solemn rites. The Church adores the crucified Lord. The altars stand the mournful bare. The fast of the Passion's day. Its 4th-century fast is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-holy-saturday: A 1913 entry on Holy Saturday — the tomb's silence. Henri Leclercq unfolds its ancient rites. The Church waits the rising Lord. The Paschal fire crowns the night. The vigil of the Resurrection's dawn. Its Exsultet is famed.

catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-o-kane-m: A 1913 entry on Murray — the American historian. Thomas Meehan honors his famous works. His pen chronicled the Irish in America. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jubilate-sund: A 1913 entry on Jubilate Sunday — the Easter season's day. George Cyprian Alston unfolds its liturgical place. The choirs sing the joyful psalms. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maria-cosway: This 1913 reference article on Cosway — the Anglo-Italian artist. George Williamson honors her famous miniatures. Her brush graced the London salons. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maundy-thursd: A 1913 entry on Maundy Thursday — the Holy Week day. Henri Leclercq unfolds its liturgical lore. It hallows the Last Supper's night. The Church keeps the ancient use. The altars know its rites. Its 1907 study is famed. Its mandatum rite is famed.

catholic-encyclopedia-1913-melo-uruguay: A 1913 entry on Melo — the Uruguayan diocese. Andrew MacErlean gives its founding story. Its bishops guard the northern flock. The entry keeps its modest record. A see of the South American east. Its 1955 founding is famed. Its bishops are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-natal-day: The Church calls a saint's feast his natal day, his birthday into heaven, the day of his death. This entry explains the term, its history, and its liturgical meaning. Dying as a second birth: the martyrs' feasts were the first natal days celebrated.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-new-year-s-da: New Year's Day is the feast of the Circumcision and, since antiquity, of Mary the Mother of God. This entry explains its liturgy, its history, and its customs. The year begins at Mary's side: the octave day of Christmas honors her motherhood.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-norway: Norway was converted by St. Olaf, kept the faith for five centuries, then lost it to the Lutheran Reformation. This entry covers its Catholic history, its shrines, and its modern revival. The land of the midnight sun and the martyr king.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-our-lady-of-a: This entry profiles the shrine of Our Lady of Ambronay, tracing its pilgrims, its miracles, and its place in French devotional life as the 1913 editors recorded it. A compact sketch from the encyclopedia's French gallery, preserved among its Marian shrines.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-palm-sunday: Palm Sunday opens Holy Week with Christ's triumphal entry into Jerusalem. This entry explains its liturgy, its procession, and its history. The king acclaimed, the cross ahead: its blessed palms become next year's solemn Lenten ashes quite unfailingly each year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paraguay: Paraguay was the land of the Jesuit reductions, the famous missions among the Guaraní. This entry covers its history, its dioceses, and the reductions' legacy. The faith in the land of the great river: its reductions were a Christian utopia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-passion-sunda: Passion Sunday is the fifth Sunday of Lent, when the crosses are veiled and the Church turns toward Calvary. This entry explains its liturgy, its customs, and its name. The fortnight of the Passion begins: its veils hide the crucifixes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-patrick-murra: This biographical entry profiles Patrick Murray, an Irish theologian of the 1800s, tracing his career, his teaching at Maynooth, and his writings as the 1913 editors recorded them. A compact life from the encyclopedia's Irish gallery, preserved among its records of Maynooth's learned professors.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-guilla: Frédéric Le Play was the sociologist who studied working-class families across Europe. This entry covers his career, his method, and his Catholic social thought. The father of family sociology: his patient monographs mapped all Europe's working households in loving detail.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-reductions-of: The Reductions of Paraguay were the Jesuits' Indian republic. This entry traces their founding, their glory, and their ruin. The utopia of the Guaraní: their ordered villages sang the Catholic faith in Guaraní tongue and song and prayer and work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sainte-anne-d: Sainte Anne d'Auray is the shrine of the Breton pilgrims. This entry covers its basilica, its pardons, and its history. The grandmother's shrine of Brittany: its great pardons draw the Bretons in Morbihan's fields in July's feast of the saint.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sir-john-char: Sir John Charles Day was the judge of the commercial court. This entry notes his bench, his cases, and his fame. The justice of the City merchants: his stern court served the commerce in the 1880s' London in the City.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sunday: Sunday is the Lord's Day of rest. This long entry examines its Sabbath, its Mass, and its law. The first day of the Christian week: its holy rest crowned the faithful in the 300s of the Church in the empire.

demetrius-a-play: Schiller's unfinished final play dramatizes the mysterious False Dmitri, who claimed the Russian throne in the Time of Troubles. Though death left it incomplete, the surviving scenes show the master's power undimmed. A fascinating fragment from the summit of German drama.
dennison-grant-a-novel-of-to-day: Robert Stead's Dennison Grant: a novel of to-day. The Canadian West in fiction. A popular tale of its time. Western Canada's story, the Canadian West in popular fiction, a tale of its time, western Canada's story.

doe-osti-3028534-electrify-monterey-bay: Monterey Bay got electrified, and this DOE text covers the bay project. The pages detail the findings. The energy folks get their data. The bay was Monterey. The data were energy. The Bay were Monterey. The project were bay. The data were DOE.

early-kings-of-norway: Thomas Carlyle's 1875 history of Norway's early kings: Harald Fairhair, Olaf the Saint, and the Viking age. Thunderous and vivid in his prophetic style, it brings the sagas to life. History as epic poetry. Carlyle's Norse heroes stride through these pages like giants.
euripides-alcestis-murray:
Euripides staged Alcestis in Athens in 438 BCE, his earliest surviving play. Gilbert Murray translated the Greek tragedy into English verse. King Admetus may escape death if another person dies in his place.

His wife Alcestis alone accepts the bargain, and the household mourns her deeply. Heracles arrives as a guest, learns the truth, and wrestles Death for her. The play blends grief, gratitude, and an almost comic rescue. It was performed in the slot usually given to a satyr play. Murray's graceful verse keeps its strange, gentle mood intact for English readers.
euripides-electra-murray:
Euripides wrote his Electra around 413 BCE, retelling a story Sophocles also staged. Gilbert Murray translated the tragedy into English verse. Electra lives in exile, married off to a poor farmer, while her mother rules with Aegisthus.

Her brother Orestes returns in secret, and recognition slowly dawns between them. Together they plan the killing of their mother Clytemnestra and her lover. Euripides makes the revenge feel squalid rather than heroic, questioning its justice. Peasant decency contrasts sharply with royal crime throughout. Murray's version brings out the play's bitterness and pity in equal measure.
euripides-hippolytus-bacchae-murray:
Gilbert Murray translated two of Euripides' darkest tragedies in this pairing. Hippolytus dates to 428 BCE, while The Bacchae was produced after the poet's death. Both plays show gods punishing humans who refuse them honor.

Hippolytus spurns Aphrodite, and his stepmother Phaedra's desire destroys them both. In The Bacchae, Dionysus returns to Thebes and drives its women into frenzy. King Pentheus, who denies the god, is torn apart by his own mother. Euripides treats divine power as beautiful and terrifying at once. Murray's verse versions long introduced English readers to these unsettling masterpieces.
euripides-iphigenia-tauris-murray:
Euripides wrote Iphigenia in Tauris around 414 BCE, late in the Trojan War cycle. Gilbert Murray translated the play into English verse. Iphigenia, thought sacrificed by her father, actually serves Artemis in a distant land.

As priestess she must prepare captured strangers for sacrifice on the altar. Two Greeks arrive, and one proves to be her brother Orestes. Brother and sister plot an escape with the goddess's statue in hand. Unlike most tragedies, the play ends in rescue and reunion. Murray renders its suspense and tenderness with unusual charm. Athena herself arrives to bless the escape at the close.
euripides-medea-murray:
Euripides staged Medea in Athens in 431 BCE, at the start of a long war. Gilbert Murray translated the tragedy into English verse. Jason has abandoned Medea, his foreign wife, to marry a Corinthian princess.

Medea pleads, schemes, and finally takes a revenge that still shocks audiences. She kills the princess, the king, and her own two children. Euripides gives her arguments so strong that Jason looks small beside her. The play asks what a wronged outsider owes to law or mercy. Murray's translation carried its power to generations of English readers.
euripides-rhesus-murray:
Rhesus is a short tragedy of a night raid during the Trojan War. Gilbert Murray translated the play, which tradition assigns to Euripides. Modern scholars often doubt that Euripides actually wrote it.

Thracian king Rhesus arrives to aid Troy and camps outside the city walls. Odysseus and Diomedes slip through the dark and kill him in his sleep. A charioteer survives to accuse Hector of betrayal and treachery. The action stays tight, nocturnal, and full of confused alarms. Even as a lesser work, it shows how Greek dramatists mined the Iliad for fresh scenes.
euripides-trojan-women-murray:
Euripides produced The Trojan Women in 415 BCE, while Athens was fighting its own brutal war. Gilbert Murray translated the tragedy into English verse. Troy has fallen, and its royal women wait to be handed to Greek masters.

Hecuba, the widowed queen, watches every remaining hope stripped away. Cassandra is dragged off, Andromache loses her small son to murder, and Helen pleads for her life. Almost nothing happens except suffering, speech by speech. That stillness is the point, and the accusation. Murray's version became famous as an anti-war statement in its own right.
extracts-from-the-diary-of-william-bray: Extracts from the diary of William Bray, the antiquary who deciphered Pepys's shorthand. Quiet, observant, and full of 18th-century detail, it records a scholar's life. A gentle pleasure for lovers of the period. Bray's quiet industry preserved Pepys for posterity.

foul-play: Foul Play is a rousing adventure by Reade and Boucicault. Dark shipwreck, black villainy, and true love drive the plot. The Victorian thriller never once slows its headlong pace. First-rate sensation fiction at its very best.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BeckRay_Beck_Ra:
More than three years after the assassination, the FBI's Dallas office still carried an open subject line: Assassination of President John F. Kennedy. This memorandum, dated February 23, 1967, went to SAC Gordon Shanklin, the special agent in charge at Dallas, under file 89-43.

The sender's name is garbled in the scan, a reminder of the condition of much of the released paper. Dallas was where the crime happened, and its office held the local file that every new lead, letter, and claim still entered. The single memo is preserved as a page of that file's long afterlife.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BertrandClayDoc:
Clay Bertrand was the name Jim Garrison's investigation chased through New Orleans: the alleged alias of Clay Shaw, the businessman Garrison put on trial for conspiring to kill President Kennedy. These research notes, dated November 23, 1971, come from a researcher's work on that matter after the trial had ended.

The notes record that Ed Planer confirmed Jesse Core appeared in preserved Johann Rush footage, film connected with Dealey Plaza on the day of the assassination. They also record meetings with Garrison himself. Research notes like these are the workshop floor of assassination scholarship: half-checked leads, names, and film references kept for later use.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-MarcusRay_Marcu:
Raymond Marcus published 'Truth vs. Political Truth' as a collection of essays, and this is volume one, dated August 2001. Marcus writes about media elites and how they shape public opinion. His central subject is the assassination of John F. Kennedy and the way it has been covered.

Marcus was a longtime researcher who argued that the press protected the official account. The essays measure news coverage against the evidence as he read it. For readers, the volume offers one researcher's case that political convenience, not proof, settled the story in print. It appeared nearly forty years after Dallas, in a debate that had by then moved from commissions to talk shows and the early internet.
gower-latin-works-macaulay:
George Macaulay's Complete Works of John Gower gathered the poet's writings in four volumes at the turn of the century. Volume Three, from 1902, prints Gower's Latin works with notes. Gower wrote in three tongues, and Latin was his language of public warning.

The chief work here is the Vox Clamantis, the Voice of One Crying, on the Peasants' Revolt of 1381 and the sins of every rank. The Cronica Tripertita treats the fall of Richard II. Shorter Latin poems fill out the volume. Macaulay's editing let English readers meet the stern moralist behind the gentle love poet of the Confessio.
heimskringla-or-the-chronicle-of-the-kin: Written around 1230 by the Icelandic chieftain Snorri Sturluson, this is the great saga-history of Norway's kings. From legendary founders through Olaf the Saint to the Battle of Hastings, Snorri mixes myth, poetry, and hard politics into gripping prose. It is our main source for the Viking Age, and its tales of voyages, feuds, and doomed kings read like the world's first great historical novel.
how-to-live-on-24-hours-a-day: Arnold Bennett's 1910 self-help classic: how to live fully on twenty-four hours a day. Practical, witty, and wise, it taught clerks to claim their evenings. The most readable time-management book ever written. Bennett's advice is as fresh as when it was written.
if-i-may: A. A. Milne's If I May gathers his whimsical Punch essays — on holidays, heroes, and the small absurdities of life. His light touch never fails. The perfect bedtime book for grown-ups. Crickets, cousins, and railway carriages all amuse his gentle pen.
ivanoff-a-play: Chekhov's 1887 early play about Ivanov, a landowner sinking into despair and debt. Rawer than his later masterpieces but full of their themes, it shows his genius forming. The young Chekhov finding his voice. Melodramatic in places, but the despair is real and the characters breathe.
keeping-fit-all-the-way:
Keeping Fit All the Way is Walter Camp's book on how to obtain and maintain health, strength, and efficiency. Camp, the famous Yale football coach, wrote it for general readers in 1919. A front photograph shows Camp himself beside ex-President Taft and Colonel Ullman. The three are named pioneers of senior service, the book's program for older men.

Part Two presents the Daily Dozen, Camp's short set of daily exercises. The exercises were devised for busy men who had no time for long training. Camp argues that fitness is a duty, not a hobby, in work and war alike. The book closes with the American Citizen's Creed. It remains the classic statement of Camp's daily-dozen plan.
laugh-and-play:
E. Stuart Hardy made Laugh and Play as a book of original stories for children. Ernest Nister published it in London, with Dutton in New York. Hardy also drew its many pictures.

An opening verse urges children to laugh and play all day. Tears and sighs, it says, make the sky grey. The stories follow that bright advice in tone. Pictures and tales work together on each page. The book was printed in Bavaria, as many fine color books then were. Short, cheerful pieces suit reading aloud to young children. Hardy's pictures give each small tale a friendly face.
little-bear-at-work-and-at-play:
Frances Margaret Fox continues her Little Bear stories here. Warner Carr illustrated this volume of animal tales. Fox dedicates it to girls of Martha Cook Dormitory, Ann Arbor. They earned the honor by loving Little Bear, she writes.

Stories show Little Bear bragging, refusing work, and learning to swim. Mother Skunk helps him in one early adventure. A lost otter baby and a school visit vary the fun. Three bears come to breakfast before his surprise party closes it. Little Bear's promise and three visiting bears fill later chapters. When Mother Skunk helped him opens the animal lessons.
little-folks-astray:
Sophie May published this children's book in 1872. She addresses parents directly before the story begins. The Parlin and Clifford children return from earlier books here. They refused to stay asleep and came downstairs again, she jokes.

Fly Clifford expects to stand in the middle of everything. Grandma Read will talk her down with Quaker speech. Aunt Madge adds a story from her own childhood summer. Lessons on self-will and respect await the little listeners. A fly in a cup of milk pictures overwhelmed Fly Clifford. Elders will have their voice in this volume, May promises.
little-miss-by-the-day:
Lucille Van Slyke published this elusive heroine's story in 1919. A colored frontispiece by Mabel Hatt illustrates the volume. The prologue argues fascinating people often slip away unmet. They leave rooms or towns just before we arrive, she writes.

Miss By-the-Day was just a little seamstress at first hearing. Her odd, drawling way of speaking charmed everyone who repeated it. People smiled dreamily whenever they mentioned her name. Van Slyke had earlier written Eve's Other Children. Geordie receives the book's dedication from Van Slyke. Eve's Other Children preceded this portrait of the seamstress.
man-in-the-iron-mask-an-essay:
The Man in the Iron Mask, an essay by Alexandre Dumas, comes from his Celebrated Crimes. This set of eight volumes was issued in 1910. Dumas warns readers that this is the essay, not his famous novel. For nearly a hundred years, he says, the problem has teased writers.

Who was the masked prisoner of the Bastille, held under strange precautions? No subject, Dumas finds, is more obscure or more attractive. Pity deepens into terror as he dwells on that long captivity. He weighs the theories that historians and romancers have offered. His own elegant answer caps the argument. It is history's classic cold case, told by a master storyteller.
margret-howth-a-story-of-to-day:
Margret Howth, A Story of To-Day, is a novel by Rebecca Harding Davis. The narrator promises a story very homely and narrow in scope. She writes, she says, from the border of the battlefield. A shadow of death has fallen on the land as she begins.

Men have forgotten to hope and forgotten to pray, she writes. Against that gloom she sets the lives of mill-town workers. Margret herself is a young woman of conscience and quiet strength. Davis had already shocked readers with her tale of mill life. Here she joins factory labor to love and moral choice. The novel is a pioneer work of American realism.
martha-by-the-day:
Julie M. Lippmann published Martha By-the-Day in 1912. Her novel opens in New York on a wet November night. Young Claire Lang stands lost in the Broadway rush.

A strong woman seizes Claire and pulls her clear of the traffic. Claire takes the grip for an insult and starts a proud speech. Then she sees her rescuer is a woman, and the scene turns to comedy and the start of a bond. Martha, the day worker of the title, stands behind that rescue. Her size, strength, and plain speech set her apart from Claire's sheltered kin.
mildred-s-inheritance-just-her-way-ann-s:
Annie Fellows Johnston gathers three stories for young readers in this volume of the Cosey Corner Series. The tales are Mildred's Inheritance, Just Her Way, and Ann's Own Way. Johnston was already known for her Little Colonel books, advertised in these pages. Each title names a girl and the test she faces.

An inheritance, a stubborn streak, and a wish to go one's own way drive the three plots. Johnston wrote for girls who liked stories of home, friendship, and character. The publisher priced her books for wide family reading. The volume shows the gentle moral storytelling that made her a favorite children's author.
musicians-of-to-day:
Romain Rolland, famed for Jean-Christophe, wrote these essays on living musicians. Mary Blaiklock translated the book, issued in New York in 1915. Claude Landi added an introduction. Berlioz stands first in the contents.

Wagner gets two parts, on Siegfried and on Tristan. Saint-Saens, Vincent d'Indy, Richard Strauss, and Hugo Wolf follow. Don Lorenzo Perosi represents sacred music in Italy. A closing part weighs French music against German. Rolland writes as a novelist who loved music deeply. His portraits mix praise, doubt, and strong personal taste in a clear, warm style.
myth-and-science-an-essay:
Tito Vignoli's essay appeared in the International Scientific Series in 1885. Kegan Paul issued this third edition in London. Chapter one asks what ideas and sources make myth. Animal sensation and perception come next.

Human sensation follows, then a clear statement of the problem. Vignoli studies how mind works on what the senses give. He traces one law through myth's long growth into science. Dreams, illusions, and madness close the argument. The book treats myth not as error but as mind's first draft. It is a bold early try at a science of how humans explain the world.
nasa-tm-19650010115-inverse-compton-scat:
Frank C Jones at Goddard Space Flight Center is named on the cover of this October 1964 paper, though the scan renders his name poorly. His subject is inverse Compton scattering by cosmic ray electrons. In that process, a fast electron gives energy to a low-energy photon and boosts it to much higher energy.

Jones treats the process as a theory problem in space physics. Cosmic ray electrons move through weak light fields in space, including sunlight. Working out how much light they boost helps explain high-energy radiation seen from space. The paper gives that calculation a careful treatment.
nasa-tm-19660007950-a-digitized-spark-ch:
Charles H Ehrmann at Goddard described a new kind of gamma ray detector in this October 20, 1965, report. A spark chamber shows the path of a high-energy particle as a trail of sparks. Making that trail digital lets a computer record it directly. Gamma rays themselves leave no trail, but they can create particles that do, revealing their arrival.

Such detectors were built for satellites and high balloons. Gamma ray astronomy was a young field with few working instruments. A digitized chamber promised cleaner data with less hand work. Ehrmann presents the development for builders who would fly the next generation of instruments above the atmosphere.
nasa-tm-19660015109-the-electronics-brai:
H Doong and M Noordzy at Goddard described, in February 1966, the electronics unit that runs an X-ray telescope spectrometer in flight. They call it the electronics brain on board the experiment. Such an instrument must sequence its own work, handle its data, and answer commands from the ground. Its brain ties the telescope and spectrometer together as one system.

The catalog note says the paper covers system operation of that unit. A flaw in the logic could idle a costly experiment in orbit. Writing the operation down in full let the team test the design before flight. It also gave operators a shared picture of what the instrument would do on its own.
nasa-tm-19660021061-quasi-biennial-varia:
Kaichi Maeda at Goddard and T Suda of the Meteorological Research Institute in Tokyo studied a slow rhythm in cosmic ray counts, in this April 1966 paper. The rhythm repeats about every two years, which is what quasi-biennial means. Air temperature affects cosmic ray readings at the ground, Maeda notes at the start. A famous two-year oscillation in stratospheric winds offered a likely partner pattern.

Linking the two rhythms would tie deep space particles to Earth's own air. Ground cosmic ray records ran for decades, far longer than satellite data. If those records carry the stratosphere's rhythm, they gain a new use. The paper was prepared for a journal of geophysical research, where both fields could weigh the claim.
nasa-tm-19700025417-apollo-range-safety-:
The Mission Feasibility Branch at the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston prepared this working paper in January 1965. It sets the range safety destruct time delay for the Saturn 1B and Saturn 5 rockets. Range safety officers must be able to destroy a rocket that flies off course.

A time delay keeps the destruct system safe during the first moments of flight. The paper covers delays for flights that start with odd attitudes or uneven thrust. An addendum followed in August 1965. Rules of this kind protected the public near the launch site while the big rockets climbed away.
nasa-tm-19720005236-design-and-prelimina:
Thomas J Miller, James P Couch, and George M Prok of the Lewis Research Center designed this space radiator and reported first tests in November 1971, as NASA TM X-2401. A spacecraft can only shed waste heat by radiating it away. The radiator served an isotope Brayton power system with about seven kilowatts of electric output. It had to reject a much larger amount of heat. The design split that duty between two radiators in series.

Each radiator carried a backup coolant loop for safety. A single puncture or clog would not kill the power system. The report covers both the design and the early test results. Low temperature operation set this radiator apart from hotter designs. Such radiators were key hardware for long life space power.
nibelungenlied-shumway:
The Nibelungenlied, composed around 1200 by an unknown Austrian poet, is the great heroic epic of the German Middle Ages. Daniel Bussier Shumway's English translation is the text here. It tells of Siegfried the dragon-slayer and the fall of the Burgundian kings.

Siegfried wins the Nibelung treasure and the hand of Kriemhild, then helps King Gunther win the warrior queen Brunhild by stealth. A quarrel of queens ends in Siegfried's murder by the grim Hagen. Kriemhild's revenge, years later at the court of her new husband Etzel, drowns both courts in blood. The poem is Germany's national epic, as stark as any saga.
night-and-day: Virginia Woolf's 1919 novel, the most old-style of her books: two young London women weigh love against freedom, home against work. Katherine dreams of the stars while Mary fights for women's rights, and both must pick a path. Calm and finely drawn, it shows Woolf before she broke all the rules.
northumberland-yesterday-and-to-day:
Jean F. Terry published Northumberland Yesterday and To-day in 1913, inscribing it to Sir Francis Douglas Blake. Terry calls Blake an eminent Northumbrian, admired by the author. Chapters begin with the coast of Northumberland. North and South Tyne, then Down the Tyne, follow the rivers toward the sea.

Newcastle upon Tyne gets a chapter, and Elswick and its founder another. The Cheviots and the Roman Wall take the reader inland and back in time. Northumbrian streams, tales and legends, and ballads and poems close the contents. Pictures show Bamburgh Castle, Hexham Abbey, and the Roman Wall at Housesteads. Terry walks her home county with pride.
oliver-cromwell-a-play:
John Drinkwater wrote this stage play about Oliver Cromwell. Houghton Mifflin published it in Boston and New York. Drinkwater dedicated it to Bernard Shaw with homage. He calls Shaw the master dramatist of his age. The cast lists Cromwell's mother, wife, and daughter Bridget.

John Hampden and Henry Ireton appear as allies. Members of Parliament and the Speaker also enter. Seth and Amos Tanner give voices from below. The play treats Cromwell's rise and the Civil War era. Drinkwater writes history as intimate stage drama. It suits readers who like plays about power and faith.
oscar-or-the-boy-who-had-his-own-way:
Walter Aimwell wrote Oscar for his Aimwell Stories, a series of moral tales for boys published in Boston in the 1850s. In his preface he states the design plainly. Oscar is a bright but headstrong boy, over-indulged by his parents. He usually manages to have his own way by hook or by crook.

The story exhibits the bad consequences of a wayward and lawless spirit, and of sliding into indolent, untruthful, and disobedient habits. Other lessons of scarcely less importance are intermingled, the preface promises. Aimwell's method is the period's own: an attractive narrative of a boy's scrapes and winter scenes on Boston Common, engineered so that young readers absorb the warning while enjoying the tale.
podcast-joerogan-Gm8xFaM-raY:
Sam Harris returns for episode 641 of the Joe Rogan Experience, a middle entry in their long series of talks. Harris, the philosopher and neuroscientist, had by then published widely on religion, ethics, and the mind. His Rogan visits often become the show's most argued-over hours.

The two test their views on free will, moral truth, and how a person should live without faith in old doctrines. Harris keeps his cool, exact manner while Rogan answers from gut and practice. The episode shows their pairing in balance, before later years made Harris a more polarizing figure in Rogan's world.
podcast-joerogan-nWY_BXHZNAY:
Author Graham Hancock returns to Joe Rogan for episode 2051 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Hancock is the best known voice for the claim that a high culture fell in the Ice Age. His books and his TV series made the case to a vast crowd.

Hancock gives Rogan his latest form of the case, from new sites to new scans. He argues the proof grows each year while the experts look away. Rogan gives him the long form to lay it all out. Listeners get the claim whole from its top teller. The library keeps the episode as a record of his stated case.
podcast-joerogan-v2oBLSDCZaY:
Thomas Campbell returns to the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 2541, a second long pass at his My Big TOE theory. Campbell, a physicist who worked on missile defense and NASA projects, argues reality is virtual. His model puts consciousness at the center of everything that exists.

Campbell restates the theory in fresh terms and answers the questions his first visit raised. He explains how a computing consciousness could render the world we touch. Rogan probes the testable parts and the spiritual ones. Open-minded listeners get a fuller map of a claim that physics and mysticism rarely share.
poems-by-the-way:
William Morris wrote the poems collected as Poems by the Way, first printed in 1891 and reprinted in a second edition by Longmans, Green in 1896. Morris, famous as a designer, craftsman, and socialist thinker, wrote verse all his life in a deliberately old-fashioned, story-loving style. The title means poems written along the way, beside his larger work, and the contents range widely.

Northern tales lead the list, with the wooing of Hallbiorn the Strong and Iceland First Seen reflecting Morris's love of the sagas. Love lyrics, battle pieces, and songs of labor follow, including the Message of the March Wind. The Voice of Toil, and the God of the Poor, where his politics enter the poetry openly. The book is a good single doorway into Morris the poet, minor works handled with major craft.
shelley-an-essay: Francis Thompson's 1908 essay on Shelley, a poet's tribute to a poet. Thompson, himself a visionary Catholic lyricist, finds in Shelley a kindred spirit of beauty and rebellion. Rich, strange, and brilliant, it is criticism as poetry.
sketches-by-boz-illustrative-of-every-da: Dickens's first book, the 1836 sketches that introduced "Boz" to London. Street vendors, cab drivers, cheap theaters, and parish beadles parade through these sharp, funny vignettes of city life. Young, hungry, and brilliantly observant, the twenty-four-year-old Dickens is already unmistakable on every page.
thackeray: Thackeray, G. K. Chesterton's study of the novelist. The critic on Thackeray. This book preserves that essay. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
the-black-bearded-barbarian-the-life-of-: The life of George Leslie Mackay, the Canadian missionary who brought Christianity and dentistry to Formosa (Taiwan) in the 1870s. His adventures among headhunters, told by Margaret MacGregor, make thrilling reading. A remarkable true story of courage. He faced headhunters and plague with equal courage, and the Formosans loved him for it.
the-broad-highway: The Broad Highway, Jeffery Farnol's Regency romance. Its highway adventure unfolds. This book preserves that novel. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
the-days-before-yesterday: The Days Before Yesterday recalls the bright Victorian high life. The writer looks back fondly on a vanished glittering world. Rich stories and portraits fill the pages. A fond look at days gone by, full of color.
the-foundations-an-extravagant-play: Galsworthy cuts loose in this wild play of ideas. Modern England gets a thorough roasting. Satire on a grand, extravagant scale, satire on a grand scale, Galsworthy's wildest, extravagant and sweeping, mocking modern England, Galsworthy's wildest stage work.
the-gilded-age-a-tale-of-today: Mark Twain and Charles Dudley Warner's 1873 Gilded Age: the novel that named an era. Washington lobbyists and get-rich schemes. The first great American satire. A classic, the novel that named an era, washington schemes and railroad fortunes, the first great American satire.
the-king-s-highway: The King's Highway is a lively romance of the open road. Its travelers meet with adventure along the old coaching highway. Highwaymen, lovers, and wanderers cross paths by moonlight. A spirited tale of old England.
the-round-up-a-romance-of-arizona-noveli: A Western romance novelized from Edmund Day's hit stage melodrama, set on the Arizona range. Cowboy heroics, a plucky heroine, rustlers, and a rousing round-up drive the plot, with all the broad emotion of the theater intact. It is popular entertainment from the heyday of the Western, when the cowboy was America's favorite hero.
to-him-that-hath-a-tale-of-the-west-of-t: Ralph Connor's To Him That Hath: a tale of today's West. The popular novelist's Western. Earnest and stirring. A favorite of its day, connor's modern West, earnest and stirring, a popular favorite, Connor's West, today's West.
toasts-and-forms-of-public-address-for-t: William Pittenger, the Andrews raider turned preacher, offers toasts and forms of public address for all who wish to say the right thing — weddings, banquets, funerals, and public days. Model speeches show the way for nervous orators. A handbook of Victorian eloquence and good manners.
tono-bungay: H. G. Wells's 1909 novel follows George Ponderevo from a struggling youth to riches built on a worthless patent medicine called Tono-Bungay. Part social satire, part portrait of Edwardian England's money fever, it charts how advertising and ambition hollow out a man's soul. Wells called it his most ambitious novel, and its diagnosis of empty prosperity still bites.
verses-and-rhymes-by-the-way: The writer known as Norah gathers her poems and rhymes — light verse on travel, nature, and everyday moments noticed along the way. Unpretentious and musical, the collection is the work of a gifted amateur writing for pleasure. Readers who enjoy gentle, old-fashioned poetry will find much to like.
wallenstein-s-camp-a-play: Schiller's Wallenstein's Camp — the lively prologue to his great Wallenstein trilogy — shows the imperial general's soldiers carousing, grumbling, and boasting. In one bustling act, the whole Thirty Years War comes alive through its common fighters. A brilliant curtain-raiser to a dramatic masterpiece.
